title: Future nostalgia: Europe’s unfinished song - European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: ECFR's fifth European Sentiment Compass uses 5,834 AI-moderated interviews across six countries to identify an “imagination gap”: about half the European public wants a stronger, more united Europe but cannot picture a credible route to it. The pivotal segment is “the uncertain” (roughly a third of the public), whose doubts centre on EU slowness, perceived hypocrisy — the Trump tariff deal being the emblem — and insecurity, and whose drift would hand the far right the coming national elections.

insights.claim: About half of the European public shows an “imagination gap” — wanting a positive European future but doubting it will materialise — rising to three-quarters of the pivotal “uncertain” segment, with Poland the exception at around a third.
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on pro-European politics is credibility of delivery, not hostility to integration — a different and more fixable problem than Euroscepticism.
insights.locator: Overall, about half of the European public seem to have an imagination gap.
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Asked to describe Europe today, 68% on average across six countries talk about general deterioration or loss of normality, while only 12% frame the crises as awakening or renewal.
insights.so_what: Elite “independence moment” messaging is not landing: the public reads the same events as decline by nearly six to one.
insights.locator: Each interview begins with an icebreaker question
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: On average 56% agree that Europe's future is in danger against only 21% who disagree, yet three-quarters describe a positive vision for Europe in 20 years and only around 13% hope for “less Europe” or the EU's dissolution.
insights.so_what: Outright anti-EU sentiment is a small minority even amid deep pessimism — the political risk runs through despair and abstention rather than explicit exit demand.
insights.locator: Turning to where things are heading, the AI asks
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Almost three-quarters of respondents say Europe is coping badly with its greatest challenges, and they blame national governments twice as often as European institutions and EU leaders.
insights.so_what: Cuts against the standard assumption that Brussels absorbs the blame — the accountability deficit sits in capitals, which reframes where anti-incumbent risk lands.
insights.locator: When it comes to naming Europe’s challenges
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: The useful political divide is no longer only pro-European versus Eurosceptic but whether people believe EU and national leaders can turn their hopes into reality.
insights.so_what: A new segmentation axis for reading European elections: belief in delivery, not identity, predicts which way soft pro-Europeans break.
insights.quote: Another important divide is whether people believe European leaders (EU and national alike) can turn their hopes into reality.
insights.locator: So, it may no longer be enough to distinguish
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Pessimism carries a uniquely European political risk: Americans who lose faith in the future cannot realistically demand the US be dismantled, but Europeans who lose confidence in the EU can plausibly ask for “less Europe” or their country's exit.
insights.so_what: Explains why European political risk converts faster into institutional risk than American political risk does — relevant to any long-dated EU integration assumption.
insights.locator: The people we spoke to are hardly alone in their pessimism.
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

themes.theme: Four segments and their party map

insights.claim: Respondents split into four groups: the positive (just under 20%), the negative (largest in every country except the Netherlands, close to half in France, Italy and Germany), the uncertain (around a third in most countries, a quarter in Britain) and the disconnected (around a tenth, but 22% in Britain).
insights.so_what: A ready-made segmentation for forecasting European elections — the negative bloc is already the plurality in the three largest continental economies.
insights.locator: Four tunes
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: The negative hold a near-hegemonic position in the electorates of the AfD, National Rally and Reform UK, and are also strongly present among PVV voters, the Polish right, Italy's Five Star Movement and non-voters in Italy, Germany and Poland.
insights.so_what: Maps exactly which electorates are already beyond persuasion, and shows the far-right and populist-left blocs share the same underlying diagnosis of Europe.
insights.locator: The negative
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: The uncertain are common among left-wing electorates across all six countries but also feature prominently among voters of the ruling centre-right parties in Germany, the Netherlands and Poland — making them the swing constituency that decides national elections.
insights.so_what: Identifies where the marginal European voter actually sits: inside governing centre-right and left electorates, not at the far-right fringe.
insights.locator: The uncertain
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: The disconnected make up almost a third of the UK Conservative Party's electorate, by far their largest concentration in any party.
insights.so_what: A concrete indicator of Conservative electoral weakness: a third of its base is politically disengaged rather than persuadable.
insights.locator: The disconnected
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Poles describe Europe's awakening most often (21%) while in France a mere 5% do so — the lowest of the six countries — despite a decade of Macron's calls for strategic autonomy.
insights.so_what: A decade of French strategic-autonomy rhetoric has produced the weakest public belief in European renewal of any country surveyed; proximity to the war, not elite messaging, drives optimism.
insights.locator: Respondents speak of Europe’s awakening most often in Poland
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Three overlapping dynamics are raising Europe's political salience: geopolitical upheaval bringing questions of power and vulnerability to kitchen tables, the “domestication” of EU policy into migration, climate and cost of living, and culture wars in which “Europe” is a target of the Trumpist political project.
insights.so_what: A three-driver model for why EU-level policy now moves national votes — useful for anticipating which Brussels files become electoral liabilities.
insights.locator: Three overlapping dynamics seem to be driving these developments.
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: As EU policymaking reaches into sensitive areas such as plastic straws, diesel cars and fossil fuel boilers, it tests vague pro-Europeanism against consequences people feel, which can make views more conditional, critical or ambivalent.
insights.so_what: Every consumer-facing green or migration rule carries a measurable political cost that is charged to “Europe” — relevant to the durability of EU regulatory agendas.
insights.locator: Second, the EU is becoming “domesticated”.
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Greater salience does not automatically mean less support: geopolitical insecurity can strengthen the perceived value of cooperation, as growing pro-Europeanism among Danes and Swedes suggests.
insights.so_what: A counter-case to the assumption that politicisation always favours Eurosceptics — threat perception can work the other way in frontline-adjacent states.
insights.locator: This is not to say greater salience always translates
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Far-right leaders use attacks on the EU as identity shorthand — AfD co-leader Alice Weidel has called for Germany to leave the euro zone and the Schengen area, and Polish President Karol Nawrocki attacks European “follies”.
insights.so_what: Euro-exit and Schengen-exit demands are now mainstream far-right positions in Germany — a tail risk that belongs in any long-dated euro scenario.
insights.locator: The AfD’s co-leader Alice Weidel, for example
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Pro-European leaders fail in two distinct ways: unconditional defence of the EU (Rob Jetten, Pedro Sánchez) stops them addressing people's anxieties, while trimmed pro-Europeanism (Donald Tusk, Friedrich Merz) moves them closer to the median voter but makes far-right views about Europe look normal.
insights.so_what: Both mainstream strategies currently in use are shown to lose ground with the decisive segment — a structural reason to expect continued far-right gains.
insights.locator: Pro-European political leaders often struggle to respond
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Where the euro-zone crisis hit hardest, as in Greece and Cyprus, it produced a lasting slump in public trust towards the EU — a precedent for what the current domestication of EU policy could do elsewhere.
insights.so_what: Trust damage from EU-imposed economic pain is persistent, not cyclical — a warning for fiscal-rule enforcement in the next downturn.
insights.locator: Some member states, like Greece and Cyprus
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

themes.theme: Three chords of doubt: slowness, hypocrisy, insecurity

insights.claim: Across all six countries, respondents most often name Europe's “slowness” as its most frustrating characteristic, and the uncertain raise it more than any other group — with the theme strongest in the Netherlands and Germany.
insights.so_what: Decision speed, not policy content, is the top public complaint — which makes visible procedural reform (QMV, coalitions of the willing) the highest-return political fix.
insights.locator: European slowness
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Slowness has stopped being a bureaucratic annoyance and become a measure of Europe's inability to act, explicitly linked by respondents to lost competitiveness against the USA, China and India and to being “massively overtaken technologically by Asia and the USA”.
insights.so_what: Public opinion has internalised the European competitiveness problem — which creates political room for deregulation and permitting reform that did not exist before.
insights.quote: not really able to adapt quickly enough and is being massively overtaken technologically by Asia and the USA
insights.locator: A German man, born in the 1960s, links cumbersome procedures
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Respondents spontaneously propose institutional fixes — replacing unanimity with a three-quarters majority, or letting smaller groups of countries lead where unanimity is unreachable.
insights.so_what: Public appetite for scrapping national vetoes is higher than assumed, lowering the political cost of treaty-adjacent reform.
insights.locator: Her solution is to replace unanimity
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: The EU's tariff agreement with the Trump administration has become a powerful cross-partisan symbol of European capitulation, with respondents from the German left to French Renaissance voters describing shame at von der Leyen having “caved in to the US”.
insights.so_what: Trade concessions to Washington carry a measurable and lasting domestic political cost in Europe — a constraint on how far the Commission can accommodate the US in future deals.
insights.quote: Every time the EU capitulates, it shows … we don’t want to do anything and would rather cling to the old status quo.
insights.locator: On a lack of courage, the EU’s tariff agreement
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Perceived double standards corrode credibility with left-leaning uncertain voters, captured by an LFI voter's formulation that Russia attacking Ukraine makes Russia the villain while Israel attacking Palestine makes Palestinians the terrorists.
insights.so_what: Middle East policy inconsistency has a direct domestic cost in European coalition politics, not just a reputational one abroad.
insights.quote: Russia attacks Ukraine; Russia is the villain. Israel attacks Palestine, but they’re terrorists. It doesn’t make sense.
insights.locator: On double standards
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Half of the uncertain name war and security as Europe's greatest challenge, but unlike the positive they rarely frame it through “geopolitical autonomy”, connecting it instead to dependence on America, internal divisions and the rise of the far right.
insights.so_what: The strategic-autonomy vocabulary elites use does not reach the decisive segment — defence spending needs a different public justification to hold politically.
insights.locator: European insecurity
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

themes.theme: Where hope is banked: memory and a leadership vacuum

insights.claim: Pedro Sánchez is the only European leader with cross-border pull: 8% across the six countries named him or Spain as a positive example, rising to a quarter of respondents in Italy and one in ten in France, with equal appeal among positive and uncertain voters.
insights.so_what: The most surprising finding in the study: a leader whose country lags on defence spending and who is unpopular at home is Europe's most admired figure abroad, purely on the strength of standing up to Washington.
insights.locator: One European leader bucks this trend
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Almost half of respondents (44%) cannot name any country, institution or political figure setting a positive European example; Macron manages just 4% and von der Leyen is barely mentioned at all.
insights.so_what: A quantified European leadership vacuum — the Commission president has effectively no public constituency across the six largest polled electorates.
insights.quote: Undoubtedly, there is a vacuum here.
insights.locator: Macron used to offer a similar form of leadership
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: People feel proud of Europe when collective action matches professed values — solidarity after the 2015 Paris attacks, covid vaccine distribution, the 2004 enlargement, the response to Russia's invasion — and ashamed when leaders proclaim values but fail to act on them.
insights.so_what: A testable rule for European political communication: pride is generated by demonstrated capability, not by vision statements — which means delivery events, not summits, move sentiment.
insights.locator: The pattern underneath these scattered memories
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Good news about Europe is scarce enough to stand out and be remembered: the defeat of Viktor Orban in Hungary after 16 years in government came up more than sporadically, unprompted, including among the uncertain.
insights.so_what: Single visible political wins have outsized sentiment effects in a low-good-news environment — relevant for judging the impact of upcoming European election outcomes.
insights.locator: Given how much bad news about Europe people see
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: “Future nostalgia” — borrowed from Dua Lipa's 2020 album — is proposed as the counter to backward-looking politics: not a longing to return to yesterday but a desire to regain the sense that the tomorrow people want is within reach.
insights.so_what: The paper's central prescriptive concept and the frame that ECFR will push into European political messaging ahead of the 2026-27 election cycle.
insights.quote: Its promise lies not in a longing to return to yesterday, but in a desire to gain a sense that the tomorrow people want is within reach.
insights.locator: Pro-European leaders urgently need to put Europe’s past to work
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: The prescribed message structure is a causal chain rather than an identity appeal: here is the problem you care about today, here is what we can do nationally, here is what we cannot do nationally, and here is what that combination makes possible five years from now.
insights.so_what: A concrete communications template that distinguishes campaigns likely to hold the uncertain from those that will lose them.
insights.quote: Here is the problem you care about today. Here is what we can do nationally. Here is what we cannot do nationally and where we need other Europeans.
insights.locator: To reach beyond the most committed Europe-believers
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Nostalgic politics is already winning: the AfD took the largest share in a German regional election in early September, and the same weekend Nigel Farage signed a pact with Jordan Bardella to “stop the boats” crossing the Channel as masked protesters marched on Britain's south coast.
insights.so_what: Evidence that the far-right internationale is now formally coordinating across the Channel, with a shared migration platform — raising the odds of aligned policy if both win power.
insights.locator: Far-right parties lead in the polls in several member states
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: All these far-right parties, in power, would likely attempt to enact policy agendas to weaken Europe and dismantle its frameworks of cooperation.
insights.so_what: The author's explicit statement of what is at stake in the coming national elections — institutional dismantling, not just policy shift.
insights.locator: All these parties and their many kin across Europe
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: The study rests on 5,834 AI-moderated voice and chat interviews run by Mandate Research on the Glaut platform between April 30th and May 15th 2026 across France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and the UK, averaging just under 18 minutes each.
insights.so_what: A signal that AI-moderated qualitative research is now operating at nationally representative scale — a structural change in the market-research industry's cost and speed curve.
insights.locator: Methodology
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Consent and mode data show the practical viability of the method: 5,834 of 9,757 pre-survey respondents (60%) consented and completed, and 79% chose written chat over audio.
insights.so_what: Useful benchmarks for anyone assessing AI-interview research: a 60% completion rate and a strong preference for text over voice.
insights.locator: Participants were recruited from an online panel provider
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka

insights.claim: Segmentation and the imagination-gap coding were performed by an LLM acting as a digital research assistant, reading each interview against written definitions and assigning labels — a methodological choice that makes the headline segment sizes model-dependent.
insights.so_what: A caveat worth pricing: the four-segment shares that drive the paper's conclusions come from AI-assisted coding rather than fixed survey items.
insights.locator: Each interview was allocated to one of the four segments
insights.speaker: Paweł Zerka
